In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the dermis of the mouse and rat are resistant to the carcinogenic effects of BaP and that this difference is not due to a decreased formation of BaP--DNA adducts in this tissue.

the mouse epidermis is more sensitive than the rat epidermis to the carcinogen BaP, whereas both mouse and rat epidemis are equally sensitive to the carcinogenicity of 4-(methylnitrosamino)-1-(3-pyridyl)-1-butanone.
the mouse epidermis has a higher susceptibility to BaP-induced carcinogenesis, and the rat epidermis is resistant.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the mouse is more sensitive than rat to BaP carcinogenesis.
the epidermis is a more efficient target tissue than dermis for BaP carcinogenesis.
the mouse is more susceptible to BaP-induced carcinogenesis because it has a more efficient metabolism, resulting in a greater amount of BaP metabolites that are carcinogenic and less detoxified.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are species differences in the amount of DNA adducts formed in the epidermis and the dermis, but the nature of the adducts is very similar.
the dermis is resistant to BaP carcinogenesis in both species.

the mouse skin is a better model to investigate the mechanisms of carcinogenesis of BaP, because the initial adduct formation and the subsequent DNA repair processes are similar to that in the human skin.
